n: This song of praise expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.

- *in my house*: This commitment to integrity might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters see *my house* as the king’s palace. The commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration. 

- Living with integrity means choosing a wise lifestyle.

- The psalmist hates what the Lord hates ({{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; see {{Psalm 5:5|Psalms 5:5}}; {{Psalm 11:4-5|11:4–5}}). 

- Perverse ideas come from corrupt human hearts (compare {{Psalm 18:26|Psalm 18:26}}).
The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity ({{Psalm 101:2|Psalm 101:2}}).
The psalmist promises to remove all evil from his house and the city of the Lord, which represents the entire kingdom.
The psalmist asks the Lord not to turn away (or *hide your face*). Israel experienced God turning his face away when they were exiled.
A weak and suffering person prays for the Lord's mercy on Jerusalem and for his presence with its people.

- *Smoke* is an image of the temporary nature of life ({{Psalm 37:20|Psalms 37:20}}; {{Psalm 68:2|68:2}}). 

- The psalmist’s *bones* represent his whole being (see {{Psalm 6:2|Psalms 6:2}}; {{Psalm 34:19-22|34:19–22}}).
Like *withered grass,* the psalmist senses his life fading away.
*skin hangs on my bones*: The psalmist has become very thin due to his deep sorrow (see {{Psalm 102:9|Psalm 102:9}}; {{Psalm 109:24|109:24}}).
Owls often live in deserted places, such as ruined cities. Because of this, the Bible sometimes uses the owl as a sign of ruin and desolation ({{Isaiah 34:11|Isaiah 34:11}}, {{Isaiah 34:15|15}}).
The psalmist cannot sleep (see {{Psalm 63:6-8|Psalm 63:6–8}}). Like* a lone bird on a housetop,* he feels alone and separated from both friends (see {{Psalm 88:8|Psalm 88:8}}) and enemies.
The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.
The psalmist feels that life is empty and short ({{Psalm 102:4|Psalms 102:4}}; {{Psalm 109:23|109:23}}; {{Psalm 144:4|144:4}}).
*forever … to all generations*: Human life is short and fragile ({{Psalm 102:3-11|Psalm 102:3–11}}). In contrast, the Lord remains forever and rules through every generation.
The topic changes from the psalmist’s troubles to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.
Now is the time for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see {{Psalm 75:2|Psalm 75:2}}; {{Jeremiah 29:10|Jeremiah 29:10}}; {{Daniel 9:1-19|Daniel 9:1–19}}).

When the Lord arises ({{Psalm 102:13|Psalm 102:13}}), the nations will tremble with fear because they will see his glory (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalm 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4a}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}). Rebuilding Zion and the temple shows God's glory and fulfills this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem ({{Revelation 21:1-27|Revelation 21}}).
The people of Israel were very poor and vulnerable (*destitute*) during the exile.
*Let this be written*: The written record serves as a reminder of the Lord's goodness.
The Lord will show mercy. Both Jews and Gentiles will worship him.
*His sanctuary* refers to God's holy place in heaven (see {{Psalm 92:8-10|Psalm 92:8–10}}).

Many people (both Jews and non-Jews) will worship the Lord together (see {{Psalm 96:7|Psalm 96:7}}, {{Psalm 96:9|9}}; {{Psalm 106:48|106:48}}; {{Isaiah 2:2-4|Isaiah 2:2–4}}; {{Isaiah 43:10-13|43:10–13}}; {{Isaiah 57:15|57:15}}; {{Isaiah 60:3-7|60:3–7}}).
Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.
The psalmist compares his short life ({{Psalm 102:23|Psalm 102:23}}) to God's eternal existence (compare {{Psalm 90:4|90:4}}).

- *wear out like a garment*: Unlike the eternal Creator, the created world will wear out like a piece of clothing (see {{Isaiah 40:28|Isaiah 40:28}}). 

- The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son ({{Hebrews 1:10-12|Hebrews 1:10–12}}).
The Lord’s presence provides the basis for the security and happiness of his people ({{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).

*all that is within me, bless His holy name*: {{Psalm 103:1-22|Psalms 103}} and {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}} both start and end with this promise ({{Psalm 103:1-2|103:1–2}}, {{Psalm 103:22|22}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}, {{Psalm 104:35|35}}; see also {{Psalm 146:1|146:1}}).
The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.
This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.
The Lord revealed himself to Moses in special ways to strengthen his relationship with his people (see {{Exodus 34:6-7|Exodus 34:6–7}}; {{Numbers 14:18|Numbers 14:18}}).
If the Lord were to constantly accuse or remain angry forever, no one would be left (see {{Isaiah 54:7-8|Isaiah 54:7–8}}; {{Isaiah 57:16|57:16}}).
God’s love and forgiveness have no limits and are complete.

The Lord is like a father to his children. This idea is central to the teachings of Jesus about God's fatherhood (see {{Matthew 5:43-48|Matthew 5:43–48}}; {{Matthew 6:1|6:1}}; {{Matthew 10:19-20|10:19–20}}; {{Matthew 12:50|12:50}}; {{Luke 6:36|Luke 6:36}}; {{Luke 12:29-32|12:29–32}}; {{John 8:31-59|John 8:31–59}}; {{John 15:1-8|15:1–8}}; see also {{2 Samuel 7:14|2 Samuel 7:14}}; {{Jeremiah 3:19|Jeremiah 3:19}}; {{Jeremiah 31:9|31:9}}; {{Malachi 1:6|Malachi 1:6}}; {{2 Corinthians 6:16-18|2 Corinthians 6:16–18}}).
The Lord compassionately cares for weak humans (see {{Psalm 37:2|Psalm 37:2}}; {{Psalm 90:5|90:5}}; {{Psalm 92:7|92:7}}; {{Psalm 102:4|102:4}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-8|Isaiah 40:6–8}}).
*from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends*: The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.
To obey God means to be faithful and loyal to him.
The psalmist urges the Lord's angels, servants, and messengers to praise the Lord.

- God's kingdom extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord. 

- The last phrase is similar to {{Psalm 103:1-2|Psalm 103:1–2}}.

- *Bless the LORD, O my soul!*: {{Psalm 103:1-22|Psalms 103}} and {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}} both begin and end with this commitment to praise ({{Psalm 103:1-2|103:1–2}}, {{Psalm 103:22|22}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}, {{Psalm 104:35|35}}). 

- *You are very great*: These words praise God for rescuing his people (see also {{Psalm 35:27|Psalms 35:27}}; {{Psalm 40:16|40:16}}; {{Psalm 70:4|70:4}}).

This creation hymn (see also {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalms 8}}, {{Psalm 33:1-22|33}}, {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}) praises God's goodness and greatness. The psalmist thinks about the current world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He views both creations as wonderfully and wisely made (compare {{Psalm 139:14|Psalm 139:14}}), as the work of the Lord's Spirit ({{Psalm 104:30|104:30}}; {{Genesis 1:2|Genesis 1:2}}; {{2 Corinthians 3:6|2 Corinthians 3:6}}).
The psalmist refers to two days of creation (see {{Genesis 1:1-8|Genesis 1:1–8}}), when God created the heavens and the light.
This poetic description pictures the clouds as *beams* that support the heavens.

- Wind and lightning (*flames of fire*) are described as God’s messengers. The Lord controls the wind, rain, and storms and uses them as he desires ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalm 77:17–18}}; {{Psalm 78:26|78:26}}; {{Psalm 135:7|135:7}}; {{Psalm 148:5-6|148:5–6}}). 

- The psalmist refers to the third day of creation ({{Genesis 1:9-13|Genesis 1:9–13}}). The Lord is master of water and earth.
At first, water covered the earth.
The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation ({{Genesis 1:9-13|Genesis 1:9–13}}).
The earth was made because God willed it.

The Lord set a firm boundary for the seas to protect the land. This shows that the Lord rules both the sea and the land. This idea also challenged the beliefs of the Canaanites, who celebrated Baal as the god who defeated the sea (see {{Psalm 29:1-11|Psalm 29}}).

The Lord rules over all waters, including seas, rivers, and springs on the land. He brought order to the waters that were once chaotic. As a result, the earth became a rich place for animals and people. Water refreshes the ground and provides life for birds and other animals.
The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it ({{Genesis 1:9-30|Genesis 1:9–30}}).
*for man to cultivate*: People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.
Both wine and olive oil can be misused (compare {{Proverbs 21:17|Proverbs 21:17}}), but the Lord gives them as gifts to improve life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by bread.

- The storks migrated from northern Europe and stayed in Palestine during the winter. 

- *rock badgers*: These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky areas.

- *the moon to mark the seasons*: Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon.

- *the sun knows when to set*: This poetic description reflects what people normally see. The sun goes down at a regular time each evening.
The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation ({{Genesis 1:14-19|Genesis 1:14–19}}). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.
Cycles of darkness and dawn mark the days on earth.
The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together (land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures). The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.
*teeming with creatures beyond number*: The ocean is full of all kinds of life (see {{Genesis 1:20-21|Genesis 1:20–21}}). This shows the Lord's creative work.

- *ships pass*: Commercial ships used for sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see {{Isaiah 2:16|Isaiah 2:16}}; {{Isaiah 23:1|23:1}}, {{Isaiah 23:3|3}}). 

- *Leviathan*: The psalmist describes this feared sea creature as something the Lord created and controls.
All living things depend on the Lord, who provides what they need and who has power over life and death (compare {{Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11}}).

*When You send Your Spirit*: Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew *ruakh*, which means "breath, wind, or spirit"). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal ({{Isaiah 32:15-20|Isaiah 32:15–20}}).
The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see {{Psalm 8:1|Psalms 8:1}}; {{Psalm 19:1-4|19:1–4}}; {{Psalm 24:7|24:7}}) and delights in his new creation (see {{Isaiah 65:19|Isaiah 65:19}}).
The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.
The trembling earth and the smoking mountains represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see {{Psalm 18:7-15|Psalm 18:7–15}}).

- The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation. 

- The final phrase returns to the opening words of {{Psalm 104:1|Psalm 104:1}} (see also {{Psalm 103:1-2|103:1–2}}, {{Psalm 103:22|22}}; {{Psalm 146:1|146:1}}).

The poet begins with a call to give thanks (see also {{Psalm 106:1|Psalms 106:1}}; {{Psalm 107:1|107:1}}; {{Psalm 118:1|118:1}}; {{Psalm 136:1|136:1}}). The other psalms continue with the refrain "for He is good!" The rest of {{Psalm 105:1-45|Psalm 105}} tells of God's goodness.

- This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys:

- from Ur to Canaan ({{Psalm 105:12|Psalm 105:12}}),

- to Egypt ({{Psalm 105:17|Psalm 105:17}}, {{Psalm 105:23|23}}),

- through the wilderness ({{Psalm 105:37|Psalm 105:37}}, {{Psalm 105:41|41}}), and

- back to Canaan ({{Psalm 105:44|Psalm 105:44}}).

These events fulfilled the Lord's promise to Abraham ({{Psalm 105:9|Psalm 105:9}}, {{Psalm 105:42|42}}), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering turned into glory, serves as a model of encouragement for Israel ({{Psalm 105:16-25|Psalm 105:16–25}}). 

- {{Psalm 105:1-15|Psalm 105:1–15}} (along with {{Psalm 96:1-13|96}}; {{Psalm 106:1|106:1}}, {{Psalm 106:47-48|47–48}}) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in {{1 Chronicles 16:1-43|1 Chronicles 16}}.

Psalms 105 and 106 praise God for his faithful love. Psalm 105 does this by reminding the Israelites of the wonderful things God has done. Psalm 106 does this in a different way. It reminds the Jews how God was faithful even when they forgot about him.

The events mentioned in these psalms are recorded in other books of the Bible. Those in Psalm 105 are recorded in the books from Genesis through to Joshua. Those in Psalm 106 are recorded in the books from Exodus through to 2 Chronicles.

In Psalm 105, remembering God’s covenants, miracles and laws led the Israelites to praise him. Talking about what God had done was one way to teach their children about God.

Psalm 105 ends by reminding God’s people why God allowed them to live in Canaan. They were to obey him and live as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. But they didn’t do that. They disobeyed God over and over again. They followed the practices of the nations around them instead of following the Mount Sinai covenant.

Psalm 106 tells this history. Verse 47 shows that the speakers of this psalm were living in exile. They had been forced to live far away from their land. This was God’s judgement against them for their sins and the sins of their people.

They talked about the evil things they had done for a reason. It helped them understand why God had brought judgement against them. It also helped them understand something about God. God had always remained faithful to his people. Time after time God’s people had forgotten about him. But God always remembered his covenant. He forgave his people and saved them when they cried out to him. This helped the speakers be bold enough to ask God to save them again. The speaker at the beginning of Psalm 106 was sure that God would save them. God’s people would celebrate, give thanks and praise him when he rescued them.

The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David ({{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.
The covenant is the Lord’s unbreakable promise to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see {{Genesis 12:1-9|Genesis 12:1–9}}; {{Genesis 15:1-21|15:1–21}}).

God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham's descendants as their special possession. They could live there as God's people ({{Psalm 105:44-45|Psalm 105:44–45}}; {{Genesis 12:7|Genesis 12:7}}; {{Genesis 15:7-21|15:7–21}}).
The Lord protected Israel’s patriarchs, the early fathers of the nation.
Abraham was one of the nation's prophets ({{Genesis 20:7|Genesis 20:7}}).
These verses tell the story of Joseph (see {{Genesis 37:1-41:57|Genesis 37–41}}).

- *his prediction*: Literally, *his word*.

- *the word of the LORD proved him right*: See {{Genesis 39:6-12|Genesis 39:6–12}}.
Egypt (Hebrew *Mitsrayim*) is called the land of Ham.
These verses describe Israel's suffering in Egypt (see {{Exodus 1:1-14|Exodus 1:1–14}}).
The psalmist tells the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt (see {{Exodus 7:20-12:30|Exodus 7:20–12:30}}).
*none … stumbled*: The Lord protected all of his people (compare {{Psalm 9:3|Psalm 9:3}}).

The exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God's promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob ({{Psalm 105:9-10|Psalm 105:9–10}}). Unlike {{Psalm 78:1-72|Psalm 78}}, the poet describes the Lord's goodness without mentioning Israel's history of rebellion (compare {{Psalm 106:1-48|Psalm 106}}).
The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a fire in the darkness ({{Exodus 13:22|Exodus 13:22}}).
The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.

Canaan was a land of pagan nations (see {{Psalm 111:6|Psalm 111:6}}). The psalmist might also be thinking about God's promise to Abraham ({{Genesis 24:60|Genesis 24:60}}) regarding the lands given to Isaac ({{Genesis 26:3|Genesis 26:3}}).
The Lord planned for Israel to show who he is by obeying him. Israel was to be his example among the nations.

- The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own past sins. From their humble state in exile, they asked for redemption and restoration. They hoped to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his anger. 

The psalm ends with a memory of the Lord’s past mercy and hope for renewed mercy ({{Psalm 106:44-48|Psalm 106:44–48}}). Israel failed, but the Lord remains constant. 

- Verses 1, {{Psalm 47:1-48:14|47–48}} (along with {{Psalm 96:1-13|Psalms 96}}; {{Psalm 105:1-15|105:1–15}}) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in {{1 Chronicles 16:1-43|1 Chronicles 16:1–43}}.
Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.
The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.

The story of Israel's redemption includes their sinful actions from the time of their ancestors to now ({{Psalm 106:43|Psalm 106:43}}). The themes of sin and God's anger towards sin start and end Book Four ({{Psalm 90:1-9|Psalms 90:1–9}}; {{Psalm 106:6|106:6}}, {{Psalm 106:23|23}}, {{Psalm 106:43|43}}).
The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.

*they … failed to wait*: God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (for example, see {{Exodus 15:24|Exodus 15:24}}; {{Exodus 16:2-3|16:2–3}}; {{Exodus 17:1-3|17:1–3}}; {{Numbers 14:26-45|Numbers 14:26–45}}; {{Numbers 21:4-9|21:4–9}}).
*He … sent a wasting disease*: See {{Exodus 32:35|Exodus 32:35}} and {{Numbers 11:33|Numbers 11:33}}.

- The people became jealous because they wanted the same role as the priests God had chosen (see {{Numbers 16:1-35|Numbers 16:1–35}}). 

- *The earth opened up*: See {{Numbers 16:28-33|Numbers 16:28–33}}.
*they … worshiped a molten image*: The people forgot their Savior and worshiped idols (see {{Exodus 32:1-6|Exodus 32:1–6}}).
*the land of Ham*: This means Egypt ({{Psalm 106:21|Psalm 106:21}}).

- The people disobeyed God’s command when they refused to enter the* pleasant land* (the promised land (see {{Jeremiah 3:19|Jeremiah 3:19}}). 

- *they did not believe His promise*: See {{Numbers 13:25-14:12|Numbers 13:25–14:12}}.

God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile ({{Numbers 14:26-30|Numbers 14:26–30}}). These judgments came because the people rejected God’s word ({{Psalm 106:24-25|Psalm 106:24–25}}) and provoked the Lord's anger ({{Psalm 106:28-46|106:28–46}}).
*they yoked themselves to Baal of Peor*: See {{Numbers 25:3|Numbers 25:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:3|Deuteronomy 4:3}}.
When the Israelites entered the land, they brought their idol worship with them. Their behavior stayed the same, and they angered the Lord with their actions.

Phinehas killed an Israelite man who openly turned away from the Lord ({{Numbers 25:3-8|Numbers 25:3–8}}). Because his action stopped the plague, the psalm credits him with righteousness. In this psalm he is presented as a stronger example of zeal for the Lord than Moses, who failed at Meribah ({{Numbers 20:11-13|Numbers 20:11–13}}).

Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the promised land. Instead of destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their customs (see {{Judges 2:1-3|Judges 2:1–3}}, {{Judges 2:11-15|11–15}}; {{Judges 3:5-6|3:5–6}}).
The gods of other nations were really demons (see {{Deuteronomy 32:17|Deuteronomy 32:17}}).
Idolatry is like adultery. Both make God’s people unclean before the Lord (see {{Leviticus 18:24|Leviticus 18:24}}; {{Hosea 5:3|Hosea 5:3}}).
God hated Israel's sin, just as he hates all sin.

The psalmist again talks about the Babylonian exile ({{Psalm 106:26-27|Psalm 106:26–27}}). The Lord judged Israel harshly, but he also restrained his anger, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.
When Israel fell, the destruction was not complete. The Lord had compassion on his people and left a remnant (a small group of people who remained).
*He remembered … and relented*: Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his covenant ({{Psalm 105:8|Psalm 105:8}}).
Even though the exile was harsh, the Lord still protected his people (see {{2 Kings 25:27-29|2 Kings 25:27–29}}).

*gather us*: The community prays for God to bring them back from exile (see {{Psalm 102:19-22|Psalms 102:19–22}}; {{Psalm 107:3|107:3}}; see also {{Isaiah 11:12|Isaiah 11:12}}; {{Isaiah 40:11|40:11}}; {{Isaiah 43:5|43:5}}; {{Isaiah 54:7|54:7}}; {{Isaiah 56:8|56:8}}; {{Isaiah 66:18|66:18}}).

- This doxology (a short song of praise) ends Book Four (compare {{Psalm 41:13|Psalms 41:13}}; {{Psalm 89:52|89:52}}). 

- *from everlasting to everlasting*: The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four ({{Psalm 90:1-2|Psalm 90:1–2}}). 

- *Let all the people say, “Amen!”*: The Hebrew word *’amen* means “It is true.” The faithful accept the Lord’s will during exile and his promise to be their God.

This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. The psalmist begins by urging the redeemed to praise God for his goodness ({{Psalm 107:1-3|Psalm 107:1–3}}). The psalmist then presents four examples of people whom the Lord saved from trouble ({{Psalm 107:4-32|Psalm 107:4–32}}). He summarizes the Lord’s control over everything ({{Psalm 107:33-42|Psalm 107:33–42}}) and ends with an invitation to recognize God’s loving devotion in all parts of life ({{Psalm 107:43|107:43}}).
The redeemed might be all who came out of exile.
People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.

Those who were lost in the *desert wastelands* thank God for his rescue. The* desert wastelands* might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom ({{Psalm 1:1|Psalm 1:1}}; {{Proverbs 4:10-15|Proverbs 4:10–15}}).
The psalmist does not say what caused his trouble and distress. Because the problem is not specific, people in many different situations can identify with the laments.

- God led them like a shepherd (see {{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}). 

- Verse 8 is repeated in {{Psalm 107:15|Psalm 107:15}}, {{Psalm 107:21|21}}, {{Psalm 107:31|31}}.
The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.
God’s counsel includes his instruction and will.

Exhausted from their hard work ({{Lamentations 5:13|Lamentations 5:13}}), the people *stumbled*. While this might be expected of the wicked ({{Psalm 9:3|Psalms 9:3}}; {{Psalm 27:2|27:2}}), it was different from the Israelites' escape from Egypt ({{Psalm 105:37|105:37}}).
Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.

The Lord creates ({{Genesis 1:3|Genesis 1:3}}) and sustains the universe ({{Hebrews 1:3|Hebrews 1:3}}) simply by speaking ({{Psalm 147:18|Psalm 147:18}}). When God speaks, people are also healed ({{Matthew 8:8|Matthew 8:8}}).
Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.
The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (compare {{Jonah 1:4|Jonah 1:4}}; {{Matthew 8:26|Matthew 8:26}}).
This call for public praise expands on the repeated phrases in {{Psalm 107:21-22|Psalms 107:21–22}} and {{Psalm 107:31|107:31}}.
The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren ({{Psalm 74:15|Psalm 74:15}}; {{Isaiah 35:6-7|Isaiah 35:6–7}}).
These two sections ({{Psalm 107:33-38|Psalm 107:33–38}}, {{Psalm 107:39-42|39–42}}) expand the theme of the Lord’s complete authority and power over things that humans cannot control.
God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s families and herds ({{Psalm 127:3|Psalms 127:3}}; {{Psalm 133:3|133:3}}; compare {{Psalm 109:8|109:8}}).
People often become poor when their leaders are oppressive.
The Lord rejects human rulers who act unjustly. He corrects their wrongdoing and brings justice on the earth.
The large families of the poor are evidence of God’s blessing.
Justice wins in God’s world ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}), and Israel’s history shows God’s loving devotion.
This psalm combines two parts from David's other psalms (compare {{Psalm 57:5|Psalms 57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:7-11|7–11}}; {{Psalm 60:5-12|60:5–12}}).
The psalmist finds no evidence that God cares (see {{Psalm 28:1|Psalm 28:1}}).

The psalmist starts this lament by accusing his accusers of repaying good with evil ({{Psalm 109:1-5|Psalm 109:1–5}}). At the end of the psalm, he prays to the Lord, seeking protection ({{Psalm 109:21-25|Psalm 109:21–25}}) and vengeance ({{Psalm 109:26-31|109:26–31}}).
The psalmist shows kindness and godliness (see {{Psalm 35:12-14|Psalm 35:12–14}}), but faces stubborn opposition and hatred.
The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks They say, which makes it unclear who is speaking.
The wicked person apparently held a position of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot ({{Acts 1:20-26|Acts 1:20–26}}).

Family members of people guilty of capital crimes sometimes died with the offender ({{Numbers 16:1-33|Numbers 16:1–33}}; {{Joshua 7:1-25|Joshua 7:1–25}}) or had their property taken away ({{1 Kings 21:13-16|1 Kings 21:13–16}}).
If one’s family name was blotted out, it meant there was no offspring to continue the family name or remember its history (see {{Proverbs 10:7|Proverbs 10:7}}).

Children share in the sinful condition of their parents ({{Psalm 51:5|Psalm 51:5}}; {{Exodus 20:5|Exodus 20:5}}; {{Ephesians 2:3|Ephesians 2:3}}). The speaker asks the Lord to punish this guilty person also for the sins of his family who lived before him (compare {{Matthew 23:35-36|Matthew 23:35–36}}).
The defendant committed very serious crimes that carried the death penalty and did not show even basic decency.
Cursing is the accused person’s whole way of life.
The psalmist asks God to act fairly and give people what they deserve (see {{Psalm 94:23|Psalm 94:23}}).
The Lord's reputation is important. If the wicked win, people might think the Lord is also wicked and be tempted to act wickedly ({{Psalm 1:1|Psalm 1:1}}).
Feeling vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist asks his Lord for help. The accusations have crushed his spirit and drained his physical strength.
A *lengthening shadow* suggests a temporary, empty life ({{Psalm 102:11|Psalms 102:11}}; {{Psalm 144:4|144:4}}). A single *locust* can be easily brushed off clothing.
These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.
The Lord’s servant demonstrates loyalty and obedience.
The psalmist was accused of being *clothed with disgrace* ({{Psalm 109:18|Psalm 109:18}}). Now, he asks that his accusers *wear their shame* like a piece of clothing.

- The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}; {{1 Chronicles 22:10|1 Chronicles 22:10}}), but he failed ({{Psalm 89:1-52|Psalm 89}}). This decree restores and elevates his position. 

- *The LORD*: This title represents the Hebrew name *Yahweh,* which is God’s personal name (see {{Exodus 3:6-14|Exodus 3:6–14}}; {{Exodus 6:2-8|6:2–8}}; {{Exodus 20:2|20:2}}). 

- *my Lord:* The Hebrew word *’adoni* means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist understood God’s messianic ruler (the king chosen by God) to be greater than himself. The New Testament often quotes this psalm to show that Jesus is the Messiah ({{Matthew 22:44-45|Matthew 22:44–45}}; {{Mark 12:36-37|Mark 12:36–37}}; {{Luke 20:42-44|Luke 20:42–44}}; {{Acts 2:34-35|Acts 2:34–35}}; {{Hebrews 1:13|Hebrews 1:13}}). 

- The Lord’s *right hand *represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him ({{Psalm 80:17|Psalm 80:17}}). 

Jesus claimed this position for himself ({{Matthew 26:64|Matthew 26:64}}; {{Mark 14:62|Mark 14:62}}; {{Mark 16:19|16:19}}; {{Luke 22:69|Luke 22:69}}), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having gone up to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father ({{Acts 2:33|Acts 2:33}}; {{Acts 5:31|5:31}}; {{Acts 7:55-56|7:55–56}}; {{Romans 8:34|Romans 8:34}}; {{Ephesians 1:20|Ephesians 1:20}}; {{Colossians 3:1|Colossians 3:1}}; {{Hebrews 1:3|Hebrews 1:3}}; {{Hebrews 8:1|8:1}}; {{Hebrews 10:12|10:12}}; {{Hebrews 12:2|12:2}}). 

- Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes shown placing their feet on the backs of their defeated enemies as on a footstool (see {{Hebrews 10:12-13|Hebrews 10:12–13}}).

Psalm 110 is one of the psalms that isn’t a prayer from someone to God. Instead, it announced God’s promises for a certain king from David’s family line. God would let this lord and king sit at his right hand. This meant that God gave him authority and a place of honour.

This king would be a priest forever like Melchizedek. David was lord and king. But the lord and king here was not David. No king of Israel served as a priest. Priests were from the family line of Levi. But they couldn’t serve forever because they died.

Many years later, Zechariah prophesied about someone who was a priest and a king. This person would combine the positions of king and priest in himself (Zechariah 6:13). Many Jews came to understand something about this person. They understood that Psalm 110 and Zechariah were talking about the messiah.

Jesus used words from Psalm 110 to show something. Jesus showed that he is the lord that the psalm talked about (Matthew 22:41–46). New Testament writers understood this as well (Acts 2:33–36). Jesus is the priest and king God made the promises of Psalm 110 about. The writer of Hebrews showed how this was true (Hebrews 6:20 – 7:28).

Jesus and the apostles quote this psalm to explain the unique role and authority of Jesus as the Messiah ({{Matthew 22:43-45|Matthew 22:43–45}}; {{Acts 2:32-36|Acts 2:32–36}}). The psalm also confirms God’s covenant with David. It gives hope that God will fulfill his promise in the future (see {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|2 Samuel 7:8–16}}).
The kingdom will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.

- God had made an unbreakable oath and covenant with David. When the exile seemed to end the line of kings from David's family ({{Psalm 89:38|Psalm 89:38}}), it created a crisis for God’s people. The placement of {{Psalm 110:1-7|Psalm 110}} in Book Five points again to the future of David’s line. David’s descendant must live according to God’s standard of integrity ({{Psalm 101:1-8|Psalm 101}}). His rule will also be shaped by God’s kingship ({{Psalm 93:1-100:5|Psalms 93–100}}). 

- *You are a priest forever*: The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The kings from David’s family had a limited priestly role. They supported and organized the worship of the temple. For example, David brought the ark to Jerusalem ({{2 Samuel 6:15|2 Samuel 6:15}}) and organized temple services ({{1 Chronicles 6:31-48|1 Chronicles 6:31–48}}; {{1 Chronicles 15:11-26|15:11–26}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:4-42|16:4–42}}; {{1 Chronicles 23:4-32|23:4–32}}; {{1 Chronicles 25:1|25:1}}). Solomon oversaw the construction of the temple ({{1 Kings 5:1-7:51|1 Kings 5:1–7:51}}). 

Even so, the offices of king and priest were separate in Israel. In the messianic kingdom, the king will also serve as a priest. He will be like Melchizedek, the king of Salem who was also a priest ({{Genesis 14:18|Genesis 14:18}}). The New Testament explains that Jesus Christ fulfills this new order of priesthood (see {{Hebrews 5:6-10|Hebrews 5:6–10}}; {{Hebrews 6:20-7:25|6:20–7:25}}).

- *at Your right hand*: This position brings help and protection (see {{Psalm 16:7-8|Psalms 16:7–8}}; {{Psalm 108:13|108:13}}). 

- The Lord will strike down rebellious kings. Rebellion against the Lord leads to death ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}; {{Romans 6:23|Romans 6:23}}).

The new priestly role of David's descendant does not cancel his old role as a conquering ruler. He still needs to bring the nations under his rule ({{Psalm 110:2-3|Psalm 110:2–3}}; see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}).
God’s messianic ruler wins victory with renewed strength, like a traveler who drinks from streams along the way ({{Psalm 110:3|Psalm 110:3}}).
